# Chapter 3: Prehistoric Era (290,000–5,000 BCE)

Overview

This chapter will trace the earliest examples of visual art from more than 40,000 years ago or even before recorded history began (**prehistory**). It will cover how early humans attempted to control their surroundings by, for example, painting lifelike animals on the walls of caves as seen in Paleolithic art. After which, we’ll discuss mesolithic and neolithic artworks to see how art representations changed throughout prehistory.

Objectives 

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- State the key artworks per prehistoric era

- Discuss the speculations of why experts think these artworks were created

## A. Paleolithic Era Art (40,000–10,000 BCE)

### Stone Age art 

This era includes a range of visual and symbolic forms created by humans during the **Paleolithic, Mesolithic, and Neolithic periods**. Archeologists have classified Stone Age art into four basic types, which are **petroglyphs, pictographs, prehistoric sculpture, and megalithic** art. These art forms were either applied to immovable rock surfaces, known as parietal art or were portable and called mobiliary art.  A brief explanation of each category of Stone Age art:

- **Petroglyphs** are one of the earliest forms of **Stone Age art** and refer to the cupules, rock carvings, and engravings made on rocks, boulders, or cave walls. These works of art were created by carving or incising the surface of rocks or stones using primitive tools such as sharp stones, bones, or antlers. Petroglyphs were created for various reasons, such as recording significant events, marking territorial boundaries, and as a form of communication.

- **Pictographs** refer to** pictorial imagery, idiomorphs, ideograms, or symbols** created using natural pigments or dyes on rock surfaces, cave walls, or portable objects. Pictographs were created using natural pigments such as ochre, charcoal, and manganese oxide. These works of art depict a range of subject matter, including animals, human figures, and abstract symbols. Pictographs were used for various purposes, such as storytelling, religious or spiritual rituals, and as a means of communication.

- **Prehistoric sculpture** refers to the **small totemic statuettes**, various forms of zoomorphic (animal forms) and therianthropic (animal-human hybrid forms) ivory carving, and relief sculptures made during the Stone Age. These sculptures were created using a range of materials such as ivory, bone, clay, and stone. The subject matter of these sculptures included animals, human figures, and abstract forms. Prehistoric sculptures were used for various purposes, such as religious or spiritual rituals, as objects of worship, or as decorative items.

- **Megalithic art** refers to petroforms (rocks/boulders arranged in geometric shapes/patterns) or any other works associated with **arrangements of stones**. These arrangements of stones were created for various purposes, such as marking graves, as a form of religious or spiritual worship, or as a means of communication. Megalithic art includes structures such as Stonehenge and Dolmens, which are found across Europe and Asia.

| Stone Age art represents the early human attempt to express themselves through visual and symbolic forms. The four basic types of Stone Age art, which are petroglyphs, pictographs, prehistoric sculpture, and megalithic art, are categorized based on the materials and techniques used to create them. These works of art provide an insight into the early human cultural and spiritual beliefs, as well as their way of life. |
| --- |

**Paleolithic artists** painted graceful and realistic animals on the walls of caves and carved stone statuettes of females as symbols of fertility as attempts to master their environment. Caves in southwest Europe hold some of humanity's most ancient paintings and engravings. Images often show animals and may have been ritual worship sites and many sculptures show pregnant women or exaggerated female sexuality. The **Paleolithic **sites of Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain have yielded some of the most famous examples of this type of art. Additionally, early humans carved stone statuettes of females, which were likely meant to symbolize fertility. The "Venus" figures of Willendorf, Lespugue, and Lausell are some of the best-known examples of this type of artifact.

### Cave Art - Lascaux Cave (17,000–15,000 BCE)

Lascaux Cave is situated in **southwestern France** and is a **Paleolithic **cave. This means that the cave contains some of the earliest prehistoric drawings that humans have discovered. The cave was first studied by French archaeologist Henri-Édouard-Prosper Breuil and is believed to have been used for hunting and religious rites over a long period of time.

**Description of the cave:** The Lascaux grotto consists of a main cavern that is 66 feet wide and 16 feet high. The cave is decorated with some 600 painted and drawn animals and symbols and nearly 1,500 engravings. 

**Artworks in the cave:** The Lascaux cave contains nearly 2,000 figures, which can be grouped into three main categories: animals, human figures, and abstract signs. The paintings in the cave depict numerous types of animals, such as horses, red deer, stags, bovines, felines, and what appear to be mythical creatures. There is only one human figure depicted in the cave, a bird-headed man with an erect phallus. Most of the major images have been painted onto the walls using mineral pigments, although some designs have also been incised into the stone.

**The Great Hall of the Bulls **is a section of the cave named after the large, impressive paintings of bulls that adorn its walls. Other animals, such as horses and deer, are also depicted in this section.

The top section of a passageway in Lascaux features the diptych of the ***Red Cow and the first Chinese Horse***, along with various signs. The Red Cow and the Chinese Horse are depicted in a large, concave space. The Red Cow's head and neck extend beyond the space, while the Chinese Horse has an unusually long tail. The Red Cow is depicted using progressively diluted black pigments on a red background. The Chinese Horse is created using red, yellow, and black pigments for the neck, body, and details. The paint itself was made from charcoal and minerals sourced from the earth. Brushes were fashioned from animal manes, sticks, and strips of animal skin. To create their artwork, ancient artists used a variety of techniques, one of the methods involved blowing paint through a hollow reed to create a spray effect.

**Purpose of the cave:** Archaeologists believe that the Lascaux cave was used as a center for hunting and religious rites over a long period of time. The paintings and engravings in the cave depict a variety of animals that were likely hunted by the early humans who used the cave. The presence of the bird-headed man figure suggests that the cave may have also been used for religious or spiritual purposes.

The Lascaux cave is an important archaeological site that provides valuable insights into the early human way of life.

### Sculpture - Venus of Willendorf (c. 22,000–24,000 BCE)

*The Venus of Willendorf* is an important statue from the **Paleolithic **era. It is thought to date back to 22,000-24,000 BCE, making it one of the oldest examples of Paleolithic art. It was discovered on the left bank of the Danube in Lower Austria, on August 7, 1908, during excavations led by Josef Szombathy and supervised by Hugo Obermaier and Josef Bayer. The statue is remarkably well-preserved, providing valuable insights into the art and culture of this early period.

This ancient sculpture, sometimes called the ***Woman of Willendorf*** or ***The Goddess of Willendorf***, is made from oolitic limestone. Its original meaning is not clearly understood, but there are several theories about what it might represent. 

**1**. The **religious **symbol of a goddess can represent **fertility** or a good hunt.

**2**. A **fertility **symbol may overemphasize female sexual characteristics, but it can also be a good luck charm for men.

**3**. An aspirational totem is a** lucky charm** that is believed to bring **prosperity**.

Only 4.3 inches long, the statue is an important archaeological discovery because it depicts a woman with exaggerated features, such as large breasts, stomach, and thighs. The statue is faceless, which has led archaeologists to believe that it was not meant to represent any one specific individual. The stone that it is made out of is not found in the area where the statue was discovered, leading researchers to believe that it was brought to the area by nomadic people from another location. One of the most interesting things about the *Venus **of Willendorf statue* is that it is just one of many similar statues that have been uncovered at other European archaeological sites.  We may never know for certain the actual reason why this statue was created and what it meant to the people who lived in the society that made it, but it is an important cultural marker nonetheless.

## B. Mesolithic Era Art (12,000–10,000 BCE)

The Mesolithic Era, also known as** the Middle Stone Age**, is a transitional period between the Paleolithic and Neolithic Eras. It occurred approximately from 12,000 to 10,000 BCE and was characterized by significant environmental and cultural changes. While the art of the Mesolithic Era is not as well-documented as that of the Paleolithic or Neolithic periods, some notable information about Mesolithic art can be identified.

- **Portable Art: **One of the key features of Mesolithic art is the emergence of portable artworks. Unlike the predominantly cave-based art of the Paleolithic Era, Mesolithic art includes smaller, portable objects such as carved figurines, pendants, beads, and tools made from bone, antler, and stone. These objects reflect a shift in human lifestyles as societies became more nomadic and began to engage in new social and cultural activities.

- **Naturalistic Depictions:** Mesolithic art continued to depict animals, similar to Paleolithic art, but with some notable differences. The representations became more naturalistic and detailed, showcasing a higher level of technical skill and observation. Animal forms were often depicted in motion, capturing their dynamic nature. Human figures, although rare, also started to appear in Mesolithic art, often in stylized or schematic forms.

- **Utilitarian and Ritual Objects:** Mesolithic art was closely connected to the practical needs and spiritual beliefs of the societies of that time. Many of the artifacts created during this period served utilitarian purposes, such as tools, weapons, and personal adornments. However, some objects, such as amulets or talismans, had symbolic or ritualistic significance, suggesting the emergence of spiritual or ceremonial practices.

- **Natural Materials and Techniques:** Artists of the Mesolithic Era continued to utilize natural materials found in their surroundings, including stone, bone, antler, and wood. Techniques such as carving, engraving, and polishing were employed to shape and embellish these materials, showcasing the developing artistic skills of the period.

- **Regional Variations:** Mesolithic art exhibits regional variations, reflecting the diversity of cultures and environments during that time. Artifacts found in different regions demonstrate unique artistic styles, subject matters, and materials used, indicating the distinct cultural practices and influences within various Mesolithic communities.

## C. Neolithic Era (10,000–4,500 BCE)

Neolithic people erected megalithic structures of huge stones to create an environment for religious ritual and the sophisticated measurement and tracking of celestial bodies. The earliest monumental structures were stone circles and soil mounds. It is believed the structures were used to commune with the powers people felt governed their lives. Some of these structures are Göbekli Tepe in Anatolia, Turkey (c. 9500 CE) and Stonehenge in Salisbury Plain, Southwest England.

### Stonehenge (c. 3000–1600 BCE)

### Who built Stonehenge?

The builders of Stonehenge, a prehistoric monument located in Wiltshire, England, **remain a mystery**. It is believed that the construction of Stonehenge began in the late Neolithic period around 3000 BCE and continued over several centuries. The monument was created by a community of people who lived in the surrounding area, and there is evidence of widespread trade and communication between different regions of prehistoric Britain during this time. The specific group or groups responsible for the construction of Stonehenge, however, is still a subject of debate and speculation amongst archaeologists and historians.

**The construction of Stonehenge** **consists of a circle of large stones** surrounding a smaller circle of stones and involved a variety of materials, including large stones, called megaliths, and smaller stones called bluestones. Megalithic structures are typically massive stone structures that have been used for a variety of purposes throughout history. The Stonehenge megaliths, which weigh up to 25 tons each, are made up of sarsen stones (quartzite blocks) and were transported from quarries located several miles away from the site. The bluestones, which weigh up to 4 tons each, were transported from even further away, possibly from the Preseli Hills in Wales. The transportation of these stones would have required a significant amount of labor and ingenuity. Additionally, the construction of Stonehenge also involved the use of earthworks, such as banks and ditches, which were used to shape and contour the landscape around the monument. It is likely that a large number of people were involved in the construction of Stonehenge, possibly from a range of different communities and regions. 

While the purpose of Stonehenge is still largely debated, it is widely believed that the site was used for **burial purposes**, as numerous human remains have been found on the location. Others believe that it served as a religious or astronomical site for early people in the area.

# Chapter 4: The Ancient World (5000 BCE–500 CE)

Overview

This chapter will explore the different civilizations in the Ancient World, including Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt, highlighting their notable visual art. 

(Note: We will sometimes be using the term **“Ancient Near East”** in this Study guide. “Near East” and “Middle East” essentially mean the same thing, but “Near East” is what the “Middle East” was called in the 19th century by early archaeologists when describing the ancient world in that area – the term stuck and so you will sometimes encounter it in the material we will be studying here.)

Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Identify the renowned artworks or architecture of Ancient Near Eastern and Asian civilizations

- Explain how the religion and culture of each civilization shaped their artworks and architecture

## A. Civilizations of Mesopotamia

One of the main areas referred to as the Near East is Mesopotamia, which is often considered the birthplace of civilization. It is considered part of the "Fertile Crescent" which is a natural band of rivers and fertile soil in the crescent-shaped area that supported agriculture for early civilizations. Mesopotamia is located between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers to the northeast of Egypt. Major ancient civilizations like Sumer, Babylon, and Assyria resided in ancient Mesopotamia.

Several archaeological expeditions to the Near East were launched during the 19th century in an attempt **to locate biblical cities mentioned in the Bible,** such as Nineveh and Babylon. These endeavors led to the eventual rediscovery of these ancient sites and the unearthing of a previously lost style of art.

The Sumerians (4500–1900 BCE)

Mesopotamian culture and civilization began with the Sumerians, who settled in the South near the Persian Gulf. They were the first major civilization and created various city-states for 2000 years, located along the region's rivers. Each city-state had its ruler, army, and ziggurat. 

**Ziggurats** were ancient Mesopotamian temples that were shaped like flat pyramids with steps to each side. Each ziggurat was dedicated to a different deity and served as a seat of government for a city-state as well as a visual reminder of the king's power.

The **most famous Sumerian city-states **were:

- **Uruk**, **the oldest** city in Mesopotamia

- **Ur**, home to the **legendary Gilgamesh**

## D. Ancient Egypt  (4300–30 BCE)

Ancient Egyptian civilization lasted for more than **3,000 years** and represents one of the most remarkable ancient cultures that is still being studied in the present era.  It had a wealth of resources since it was situated where the **Nile River** drains into the Mediterranean Sea. 

The Nile River's **yearly flooding** created incredibly productive agricultural land, enabling the Egyptians to produce enough food to feed a rapidly expanding population and fuel their territorial conquests.  Egyptian civilization placed a **high value on art and architecture**, **which had close links to religion**. Temple complexes built in ancient Egypt, such as those at Karnak and Luxor, for example, frequently had **distinct religious motivations for their architecture**.

### What were the primary architectural structures and artistic forms found in ancient Egypt?

Ancient Egyptian art and architecture encompassed a variety of structures and artistic forms. **Architecture included temples and tombs**, with the latter being primarily preserved due to their location above the Nile floodplain. Tombs showcased intricate **reliefs depicting scenes from earthly life **to ensure a prosperous afterlife. Temples served as sites for rituals and worship. Egyptian art comprised **sculptures, reliefs, paintings, jewelry, and hieroglyphics**. Sculptures were made from wood, metal, and stone, while reliefs were often found in tombs and often depicted historical events. Jewelry emphasized vibrant colors and intricate designs, and hieroglyphics were a written language using pictorial symbols.

Egyptian art, largely preserved in **tombs and monuments**, reflects a strong focus on the afterlife and the preservation of historical knowledge. This emphasis is evident in the earliest royal monuments, like the **Narmer Palette** from around 3100 BCE, which depict consistent royal costumes and poses that endure throughout the centuries. Remarkably, even **Ptolemaic kings**, who ruled temples 3000 years later, were depicted in similar fashion. Egyptian thought is structured around **binary concepts** such as the living and the dead, as well as order and chaos, which shaped their artistic expressions and cultural beliefs.

### The Rosetta Stone

**The Rosetta Stone** is a famous artifact that played a critical role in **deciphering** ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs. This stone was discovered in 1799 and contained a decree praising the ancient Egyptian King Ptolemy V. What made this stone so important was that the same decree was written in **three different languages**: ancient Egyptian, Demotic, and Greek. This was done so that the decree could be understood by everyone living in Egypt at that time. The Demotic language was a later form of ancient Egyptian and was closely related to the language spoken during the 26th dynasty. It was written before Coptic, which was the first time the Egyptian language was written in a non-Egyptian script derived from the Greek alphabet. The Rosetta Stone helped scholars compare the three scripts and ultimately led to the discovery of the key to understanding the hieroglyphs. It remains one of the most significant discoveries in the history of Egyptology.

### Narmer Palette (c. 3200–3000 BCE)

This stone tablet, dating back to the 31st century BCE is thought to represent the unification of Egypt under Pharaoh Narmer. On one side, there is an image of the king donning the red crown of Lower Egypt, while on the reverse side, he is portrayed with the white crown of Upper Egypt. Yet, there are other subtle symbols of Egyptian unification present here. Notably, this artifact showcases the earliest instance of the traditional Egyptian aesthetic, characterized by an art style that remained a defining feature of unified Egyptian culture for several generations. Furthermore, the Narmer Palette contains some of the oldest Egyptian hieroglyphics ever discovered, further attesting to the advanced stage of Egyptian culture during this period.

Egyptian civilization was characterized by remarkable stability, especially in comparison to the Ancient Near East during the same period, which experienced a series of overlapping cultures and upheavals. The preservation of Egyptian art and artifacts through tombs and monuments reflects their belief in the importance of preserving their culture and ensuring the continuity of their society. Additionally, the emphasis on life after death in Egyptian art speaks to the importance they placed on the afterlife and the belief that death was not the end but rather the beginning of a new journey.

### Ancient Egyptian Architecture

Their society consisted of intricate social structures, and they produced significant architectural achievements that dot the landscape of their ancient realm to this day. Certain key architectural structures were of great importance to Egyptian society: **Mastabas, Pyramids, Temples, and Obelisks**.

- **Mastabas**** **are the earliest type of **funerary building **created by the ancient Egyptians and were initially **for the aristocratic elite of society**. In ancient Egypt, the preservation of the body and the soul was crucial for ensuring a safe and prosperous afterlife. The standard tomb type used by the ancient Egyptians was the mastaba, which was a **rectangular brick or stone structure with sloping sides**. It was erected over an **underground burial chamber**, which housed the deceased's body, along with various offerings, such as food and other items. The mastaba consisted of two layers, with a chapel inside the top layer, where family members could come to bring offerings for the soul of the deceased. The chapel also housed a statue of the deceased, which was believed to serve as a physical representation of the individual in the afterlife. 

Initially, the mastaba was designed for a single person, but later on, multiple family members were buried together in one tomb. The Egyptians believed that the soul had to be maintained in the afterlife, and so family members would regularly visit the tomb to make offerings to ensure the soul's safety and happiness. 

- **Pyramids**** **were constructed to house **pharaohs' tombs** as well as act as **temples to the gods**. The ancient **pyramids of Giza**, which were constructed more than **4,000 years ago** and are still standing today, are regarded as one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. 

**The Stepped Pyramid of Djoser**, designed by Imhotep, stands at an impressive height of 200 feet and is composed of six stacked mastabas. Imhotep, recognized as the first named artist in history, held the role of a royal builder.

Unlike a ziggurat, this structure began as stacked mastabas and served as a tomb to safeguard the mummified king and his possessions, symbolizing his divine authority. It was enclosed by a 34-foot high and 5,400-foot long wall made of white limestone, making it the first Egyptian tomb constructed entirely of stone.

Notably, each face of the pyramid was aligned with one of the cardinal points of the compass, (north, south, east, west) showcasing precise orientation and meticulous planning. The Stepped Pyramid of Djoser stands as a remarkable architectural achievement and a testament to the ingenuity of Imhotep and the ancient Egyptians.

**The Great Pyramid of Giza**** **is **the oldest and largest of the three pyramids** located in the Giza Pyramid complex in Egypt. It was constructed by the Pharaoh Khufu. The pyramid was built using limestone masonry, with the original casing made of white limestone that reflected light. The Great Pyramid is a massive structure, with an estimated 2.3 million stone blocks used in its construction. The pyramid was built over a period of approximately 20 years, and was originally covered with a layer of white limestone that gave it a bright and shiny appearance. However, much of this outer layer has since been removed, leaving the pyramid with its characteristic rough appearance. The purpose of the Great Pyramid is believed to have been as a tomb for the Pharaoh Khufu, and its construction was a massive undertaking that involved a significant portion of the population of ancient Egypt. Despite its age, the Great Pyramid remains an impressive example of ancient architecture and engineering and continues to attract visitors from all over the world who marvel at its size and grandeur.

**The Giza Pyramid complex**, located in Egypt, includes the Pyramids of Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure, as well as their respective complexes and the **Great Sphinx**. These pyramids were constructed during the 4th Dynasty over a span of 75 years.

- **Khufu's pyramid** built between 2551-2528 BCE

- **Khafre's pyramid** built between 2520-2494 BCE

The form of the Giza Pyramid Complex was influenced by **Heliopolis**, which was the center of the cult of Ra, the god of the sun. Additionally, all of the pyramids were oriented towards the **cardinal points of the compass**, with temples located on the east to face the rising sun.

- **Obelisks**** **are **pointed stone pillars** that the **pharaohs, and other notable Egyptians,** **erected as monuments to their great accomplishments**. They also acted as places of **worship for the sun god Ra**, and as a form of **magical protection** for Egypt's tombs, temples, and kingdoms.

**The obelisks outside Karnak Temple** in ancient Egypt are tall, slender pillars carved from a single piece of stone. They were symbols of pharaoh's power, adorned with hieroglyphic inscriptions. **The Great Sphinx **is a massive statue of a mythical creature with the body of a lion and the head of a human. It is situated on the Giza Plateau on the west bank of the Nile in Giza, Egypt, and is believed to have been associated with the **sun god, Ra**. The Sphinx was carved from the spur of a rock and is the **largest statue** in the ancient Near East.

The Sphinx represents the combination of human intelligence with the awesome strength and authority of the king of beasts. 

Over time, the Great Sphinx has suffered damage due to erosion caused by wind and sand. Despite this, it remains a significant and awe-inspiring monument, symbolizing the power and grandeur of ancient Egyptian civilization. Its massive size and intricate details continue to fascinate historians and tourists alike, providing a glimpse into the rich and complex cultural heritage of ancient Egypt.

### The Egyptian Canon

The Egyptian Canon was a **methodical approach** to creating beauty in art that lasted for thousands of years and is still used today in art, though in a more sophisticated form. It involved placing different parts of the human body at specific points on a grid, with each body part occupying a fixed number of squares. The grid was initially drawn on the wall, and the artists followed it to create their works.

This approach to design allowed for a **consistent and recognizable style across different pieces of art**. Although proportions varied, the principles of the Canon remained consistent. The Canon of Proportions and Egyptian figures from Egypt's Old Kingdom dictated that the figures would be exactly eighteen squares tall, and this was achieved by using the grid system.

This method was a rational way of creating art and **ensured that each figure’s body part was in proportion to the rest of the body**. It was a system that was easy to follow and allowed for a consistent style in Egyptian art. 

### Ancient Egyptian Art

Three key artworks of Egyptian civilization are hieroglyphics, tomb paintings, and sculptures.** Hieroglyphics**, the ancient Egyptian **pictorial writing system** (and one of the oldest writing systems in the world), **represented words and sounds using images and symbols** and are found on the walls of every Egyptian obelisk and pyramid chamber. They range from **telling historical narratives of kingly conquests to religious tales and evocations of their gods**. 

Aside from hieroglyphics, **tomb paintings, sculptures, and reliefs** often filled the **burial chambers** of wealthy Egyptians. The paintings were richly colored and detailed with images showing the **dead's journey to the afterlife**, and sculptures often represented their idealized forms or represented specific gods and goddesses. It was believed that these paintings and smaller sculptures would become real and join the dead in the afterlife to serve them.

### Hatshepsut with Offering Jars (1479–1458 BCE)			

Hatshepsut was an ancient **Egyptian ruler** who gained the same amount of authority as any male ruler before her. She is depicted in a statue holding globular offering jars, which were used as a ritual honor for the sun-god Ra. The inscription on the statue indicates that Hatshepsut is offering god Amun “Maat”, (which means order, truth, or justice) affirming that “Maat” is the guiding principle of her reign.

Interestingly, Hatshepsut is **portrayed in this statue as a male Pharaoh**, which was not uncommon for Egyptian rulers. However, over 200 of her images were destroyed after her death. This larger-than-life-size kneeling statue, along with others in the collection, were made to flank the processional pathway along the axis of Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahri. Each statue has an inscription that includes her personal name, Hatshepsut, and/or a feminine pronoun or verb form, indicating that the masculine garb and physique were not intended to trick people into thinking she was a man. The statue was also used to connect with Egyptian spirituality and to communicate with her followers on a religious and political level.

The kneeling statue of Queen Hatshepsut was made out of **red granite,** a common material used in Egyptian sculpture due to its durability and ability to hold intricate detail. The use of this material, along with the careful carving of the statue's features, demonstrates the high skill level of ancient Egyptian sculptors. The statue was likely created using chisels and other carving tools, as well as abrasives such as sand and water to smooth and polish the surface of the granite.

**The statue of *****Khafre Enthroned*** is an iconic sculpture from ancient Egypt that depicts the Pharaoh Khafre of the Fourth Dynasty, who ruled between ca. 2520-2494 BCE. 

The statue is made out of **diorite**. The king is shown seated upon a lion-pawed throne that is carved with **symbols of royalty**. The front of the throne features lion paws and protomas, while the sides bear the symbol of the sema-tawy, which represents the unity of Upper and Lower Egypt. The back of the throne is adorned with the god Horus in the form of a falcon spreading his wings around the king's head.

The pharaoh is shown wearing a linen nemes headdress with a Uraeus, a sacred serpent **symbolizing kingship**. The statue's frontal, rigid, and bilaterally symmetrical pose gives the pharaoh a serene appearance. The subtractive method of sculpture was used, which gives the statue a block-like appearance and allows one to see the evidence of the original block. The statue looks similar to the Great Sphinx, associated with the sun god and believed to be an image of Khafre or Khufu.

The statue's importance lies in its **depiction of the pharaoh's power**, as he sits atop the throne, expressing both determination and serenity, gesturing a message of strength and control. The symbols on the throne emphasize the king's duty to bind together the parts of Egypt under his authority. The pharaoh's headdress and the falcon emblem behind it represent divine protection, which underscores his status as a ruler ordained by the gods.

**The sculpture *****Menkaure and Khamerernebty***** (2532-2510 BCE)**** **is an ancient Egyptian artwork from the **Old Kingdom period**. It is a double portrait of the pharaoh Menkaure and his queen Khamerernebty and is known for its rigid pose and frontal stance. 

- **Menkaure** is depicted with his arms rigidly at his sides, holding a baton, which is a symbol of power. 

- **Queen Khamerernebty** is shown in a similar position, embracing her husband to show they are married, yet she shows no emotion. 

The sculpture is also notable for traces of paint that are still visible. One unique aspect of the sculpture is that both figures have their left foot forward, which is typical for male figures in Egyptian sculpture but unusual for female figures, who are generally depicted with their feet together. Overall, *Menkaure and Khamerernebty* is a significant artwork that provides insight into the conventions of Egyptian art and the roles of pharaohs and queens in ancient Egyptian society.

### Akhenaten and the Amarna Period (1353-1335 BC**E)**

Akhenaten, **previously known as Amenhotep IV**, was an Egyptian pharaoh who defied tradition by establishing a new religion that believed in one god, the sun god Aten. This marked a brief religious revolution in Egyptian history, as Akhenaten abandoned worship of the old gods, especially Amun of Thebes and the sun god Re-Harakhte, in favor of Aten.

Aten was never depicted in human or animal form, but rather as a sun disk with extended rays ending in hands, representing the life-giving and sustaining power of the sun. Unlike the old gods, Aten was worshiped out in the light of day and had no carved image hidden in a dark room deep within a temple.

Akhenaten's reign also saw a **major artistic revolution**, with sculpture becoming** highly stylized and elongated**. His own body was depicted with feminine qualities, including a protruding belly, wide hips, and weak arms, which some scholars believe was a deliberate artistic reaction against the established Egyptian canon.

During his reign, Akhenaten built a new city and shrines at Akhetaten (today Tell-el-Amarna), but his religious reforms were eventually undone, and the city was abandoned. Nonetheless, his reign marks an important period in Egyptian history as a time of intellectual and philosophical revolution.

### Bust of Nefertiti (1345 BCE)

The *Nefertiti Bust* is a **stucco-coated limestone sculpture** of **Nefertiti, the Royal Wife of Pharaoh Akhenaten**, believed to have been crafted by Thutmose in 1345 BCE. It is considered one of the **most copied works** of art from ancient Egypt in the Amarna Period, and its iconic image of Nefertiti has enduring cultural significance.

The bust portrays Nefertiti wearing her signature blue headdress adorned with a **golden diadem and intricate designs**, which reflects her regal status and aesthetic appeal. The symmetrical, poised, and objectively beautiful face of Nefertiti has captured the attention of people for centuries, making it one of the world's most beloved artworks.

Nefertiti's lasting cultural relevance is reflected in the many adaptations and homages by contemporary artists around the world. However, debates surrounding her gender and racial identity have caused controversy in her modern cultural appeal. Some argue that Nefertiti's representation as a strong, powerful female figure is important, while others question whether she is being fetishized or misrepresented. Similarly, there is an ongoing debate over Nefertiti’s racial or ethnic identity. Despite these debates, the Nefertiti Bust remains a symbol of timeless beauty and cultural fascination.

### Tutankhamun’s Mask (1323 BCE)

Tutankhamun, also known as** ****"****King Tut,****"** was a pharaoh who reigned over ancient Egypt from 1333 BCE until his death in 1323 BCE. Despite his short reign, his tomb is considered one of the most important archaeological discoveries of modern times. In 1922, the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb, largely untouched since ancient times, was a **major breakthrough** in the field of archaeology.

The death mask of the Pharaoh Tutankhamun is a masterpiece of ancient Egyptian art that was created using several materials. The mask itself is made of **solid gold** and weighs approximately 24 pounds. The face of the mask is made of a smooth layer of gold, while the details of the facial features and the beard are created using **inlaid precious stones** and **colored glass**. The eyebrows are made of **inlaid obsidian**, while the eyes are made of **quartz** and obsidian with black paint for the pupils. The headpiece is made of solid gold and is decorated with scenes from Egyptian mythology. The mask was created using a technique called **repoussé**, which involves hammering gold into a mold from the back to create a raised design on the front. The result is a stunning work of art that has captivated people for decades. 

Tutankhamun became the King of Egypt at the young age of nine during the 18th dynasty of the New Kingdom. His story may have been lost to history if not for the discovery of his tomb in 1922 by the archaeologist** Howard Carter** in the Valley of the Kings. The mask, which originally rested directly on the shoulders of the mummy inside the innermost gold coffin, is considered one of the most well-known works of art in the world. Tutankhamun died at the age of eighteen under mysterious circumstances, leading scholars to speculate on the manner of his death, but the answer remains unclear. The mask is a testament to the **skill and craftsmanship** of ancient Egyptian artists and serves as a lasting tribute to the legacy of Tutankhamun, one of Egypt's most iconic pharaohs.

### How did the concept of perfect equilibrium and binary concepts influence the art and society of ancient Egypt?

As these paintings and sculptures portrayed the **perfect world of the gods** rather than the imperfect real world, art (and much of Egyptian society) was predicated on the idea of **perfect equilibrium** - using **binary concepts** such as good/evil, beautify/ugliness, life/death to inform their rituals and laws. 

Even though it lasted longer than other nearby civilizations, the Ancient Egyptians would eventually decline. Soon, they found themselves conquered by other empires over time, including the Assyrians, Persians, Alexander the Great, the Romans, the Turks, the French, and finally, the British until their independence as a modern nation-state in 1922. 

Even so, their cultural legacy was so strong that all these civilizations, and more besides, felt **strongly influenced by the accomplishments of the Egyptians**, even paying homage to them through famous architectural landmarks, such as the **Washington Monument** (an obelisk) in Washington DC, USA and the **Louvre Art Museum** (pyramid) in Paris, France.

Classical art spans the cultures of Greece and Rome and has served as the foundation of Western civilization for centuries. Classical Art, which included advancements in painting, sculpture, decorative arts, and architecture, sought ideals of beauty, harmony, and proportion, even as those values altered and changed with time. The human figure, human experience of space, and their relationship with the gods were important to Classical Art, although often also used for political propaganda. ## A. Ancient Greece: Archaic, Classical, and Hellenistic (2700–30 BCE)

Ancient Greece is often referred to as **the cradle of Western civilization**, known for its significant contributions to the arts, philosophy, politics, and more. Ancient Greek art and architecture are particularly renowned for their enduring influence on Western art history. 

- **The Archaic period** in ancient Greece **(8****th****–6****th**** centuries BCE)** is characterized by a revival of artistic **expression and experimentation** after the collapse of the Mycenaean civilization. The art of this period is characterized by a strong influence from ancient Egyptian art, with the development of the *kouros *(male youth) and *kore *(female youth) sculptures, which aimed to represent the idealized human form in a naturalistic way. Architecture during this period is also notable, with the development of the Doric and Ionic orders in temple construction.

- **The Classical period** in ancient Greece **(5****th****–4****th**** centuries BCE)** is considered the pinnacle of Greek art and architecture, with the creation of some of the most iconic works in history. This period is marked by a shift towards a more **humanistic and naturalistic style**, exemplified by the sculptures of Phidias and Polykleitos. The art of this period focused on the idealized representation of the human form, with an emphasis on harmony, balance, and proportion. Architecture during this period saw the construction of some of the most iconic structures, including the Parthenon in Athens.

- **The Hellenistic period** in ancient Greece **(4****th****–1****st**** centuries BCE)** is marked by a continuation of the **humanistic and naturalistic style** of the Classical period, but with a **greater emphasis on emotion and drama**. Sculpture during this period is characterized by more fluid and dynamic poses, as well as the use of new materials like bronze. The art of this period also saw the development of new themes and subjects, including portraiture, mythological scenes, and scenes from daily life.

- **Ancient Rome**** (753 BCE–476 CE)** was heavily influenced by ancient Greece, but developed its own distinct style and innovations in art and architecture. Roman art is characterized by a **focus on realism**, with an emphasis on **portraiture and narrative scenes**. Roman architecture was characterized by monumental structures such as aqueducts, bridges, and amphitheaters, as well as the development of new building materials and construction techniques.

### The Archaic Period of ancient Greek art

#### Mantiklos Apollo (700-680 BCE)

***The Mantiklos Apollo***** statue**** belongs to the Geometric period** of ancient Greek art, which lasted from around 900 to 700 BCE. *The Mantiklos Apollo* is a bronze sculpture created by an unknown artist named Mantiklos. The sculpture, which is approximately eight inches tall, was dedicated to the god Apollo (called a “votive offering”) in Thebes, Greece, and is now on display at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.

This sculpture is not only aesthetically pleasing but also historically significant for three reasons. 

- Firstly, it is considered one of the **masterpieces** of the early seventh century. 

- Secondly, it reflects the Greeks' increasing interest in **reproducing details** of human anatomy, such as the long hair framing the neck, the eye sockets on the triangular face, and the abdominal muscles defining the triangular torso. 

- Thirdly, it illustrates the **influence of Eastern artwork** on Greek art, particularly in the use of small portable objects like Syrian ivory carvings.

*The Mantiklos Apollo* holds great interest for art enthusiasts and historians alike. Its depiction of human anatomy is seen as a precursor to modern art, and its influence on the development of Greek art is a testament to the power of cross-cultural exchange.

#### Kouros

***Kouros *****sculptures are a type of ancient Greek artwork that date back to the Archaic period in Greece**, 800–480 BCE. This period is known for its significant developments in art, architecture, and politics, including the rise of the polis, or city-state, and the creation of monumental stone temples and sculptures. 

The *kouros *was a popular form of sculpture during this time, and many examples of these works have been found throughout Greece. These free-standing sculptures depict nude male youths and were not meant to represent any one person but rather the concept of youth itself.

*Kouros *statues were used in a variety of settings, such as dedications to the gods in sanctuaries, and as grave monuments. They were often made of **marble or limestone** and were highly valued for their **artistic and symbolic significance**. 

Influenced by the Egyptian style of sculpture, a standard *kouros *statue would be depicted standing with his left foot forward, arms at his sides, and looking straight ahead sometimes with a slight, enigmatic smile on his face. This smile is known as the **"****archaic smile,****"**** **which was a common feature in early Greek art. The "archaic smile" is characterized by a slight upward curve of the lips, which is meant to convey a sense of idealized beauty and serenity. *Kouros *sculptures were highly influential in ancient Greek art and continue to be admired for their beauty and artistic significance to this day.

#### Peplos Kore

**A *****kore *****is a type of ancient Greek sculpture from the Archaic period specifically depicting a young woman.** The word "kore" means "young woman" or "girl" in Greek. These sculptures were often used as votive offerings to the gods or as grave markers.

One interesting fact about *korai *(plural of *kore*) is that many of them were buried by the Athenians to protect them from being destroyed by the Persians in 480 BCE during the sacking of the Acropolis. And they remained buried until being rediscovered some 2,000 years later.

*Korai *typically stand frontally with their feet together, arms at their sides or pulling at their skirts, and looking directly at the viewer. They may also be holding an object with one outstretched hand. One of the defining characteristics of *korai *is their dress, which is often made up of multiple layers of fabric. The fabric can conceal or reveal the body underneath and is draped in such a way that it creates a variety of different textures and pleats.

## C. The Minoan Civilization (2700–1500 BCE)

The Minoan civilization emerged on the island of Crete around 2700 BCE during the Bronze Age, spreading across the Mediterranean and gradually forming a complex society by 3000 BCE. 

The Minoan society was rich in trade, art, and writing. Many were artists, seafarers, and traders, and they traveled the Mediterranean, exchanging language, arts, and goods with people from around the ancient world, particularly ancient Egypt. The most important **trade goods** for the Minoans seem to have been **saffron **and **tin**.

It was Sir Arthur Evans who discovered the evidence of their existence in 1900 on the island of Crete, which helped us understand the world of Minoans and their civilization.

### Minoan Art

Minoan art tells us about their culture but, as we cannot yet read Minoan records, it is difficult to know the exact meaning behind their art, though there are various interpretations. Most Minoan paintings take the form of frescoes, which can be seen in homes, palaces, and even in the throne room in Knossos. 

***The Bull-leaping fresco*** from the east wing of the palace of **Knossos **is 30.8 inches high and 41.1 inches long. And the people are color-coded similar to the Egyptian style.

It is not known if bull-leaping was a sport, a rite of passage, or some kind of religious ceremony. 

*Bull-leaping fresco*, c. 1400 BCE

Minoans seemed to have favored nature scenes in their art with frescoes depicting the natural world, animals, landscapes, and sea creatures. ***The Dolphin Fresco***, originating from the **Palace of Knossos around 1500 BCE**, is an example of the Minoans' exquisite fresco paintings. 

These paintings adorned the walls of their palaces and were created using a unique technique: the **fresco method**, which involved **applying color pigments onto wet lime plaster**. As the paint seeped into the plaster, it became embedded and secured, ensuring its longevity and resistance to fading over time. *The Dolphin Fresco*, with its **vibrant colors and skillful execution**, showcases the Minoans' mastery of this artistic technique, allowing their intricate and captivating designs to endure for centuries.

### Minoan SculpturesFor their sculptures, Minoans used stone and bronze, sometimes other materials. Some of the bronze works portray women in skirts, with at least one exposed breast,  men in loincloths, and some animal figurines were also found.  

***The Snake Goddess***, created around 1600 BCE, is a nearly **13.1”**** tall **figure of a **woman holding a writhing snake in either hand**.  The figure is known for the intricate, refined details of her clothing (**layered skirt**, **exposed breasts**) and the **intense glare staring straight ahead**.

When creating human figures in sculpture, the Minoans stuck to the same tall, slender figures similar to their paintings. Some of the almost life-size nude sculptures are carved from stone and layered with ivory and gold, very similar to later Greek sculptures, hinting that the Minoans may have been the early influencer or originator of the ***chryselephantine*** style in which the “flesh” of the sculpture was made of ivory and the drapery of gold.

### Minoan Pottery

***The Minoan Octopus Jar***** (1500-1450 BCE)** was a significant artifact that symbolized the deep reverence the Minoan culture had for the sea. This jar was created as a **celebration of the marine world**, with the octopus holding great importance as a symbol within Minoan society. The intricate design and craftsmanship of the jar depicted the octopus in a visually captivating and **symbolic manner**, reflecting the Minoans' connection to and appreciation for the maritime environment that played a vital role in their lives. The decoration on Minoan pottery was diverse and intricate. 

*Kamares ware*, known for its **abstract patterns and striking color contrasts**, showcased the Minoans' fascination with aquatic life, featuring sea creatures like the octopus and dolphin. This gave rise to the "Marine Style" designation. Another decorative style emerged later, known as the "Palace Style," characterized by symmetrical and stylized arrangements of plants, flowers, and sea life. These decorative motifs were popular in Minoan trade, evident from archaeological discoveries across the Aegean islands and beyond. 

### So, what caused the decline of Minoan civilization in the 15th century BCE? 

The Minoan civilization started to decline sharply around 1450 BCE, though the exact cause is still debatable, and nothing has been proven. Many believe that the advent of the Iron Age played a major role as people no longer needed so much bronze, leading to the decline of the Minoan bronze-based economy. Others believe that the rise of Mycenaean civilization and their dominance of the island of Crete a few decades later contributed to the decline of Minoan civilization. Another explanation is the catastrophic explosion of the volcanic island of Thera, modern-day Santorini, which could have produced a tsunami of epic proportions that destroyed the island of Crete and its citizens.

## D. The Mycenaeans Civilizations (1600–1100 BCE)

During the Late Bronze Age, the ***Mycenaeans ***were at their height in the Peloponnese Peninsula of southern Greece between 1600 and 1100 BCE. They were a warrior society that conquered their neighbors and raided settlements by both land and sea, gradually building their wealth and power. They controlled more than one hundred city-states across the Peloponnese and were the most powerful Aegean civilization before the rise of ancient Greece. **Mycenae **was the most dominant among Mycenaean city-states. 

### Mycenaean Art and Metalwork

Mycenaeans adopted many traditions from the Minoans and excelled at creating frescoes, pottery, jewelry, armor, and sculptures. While Minoan art is known for being inspired by nature, Mycenaean art is **more stylized and has more abstract** **forms and images**. Like Minoans, they decorated the walls of palaces, private homes, and other buildings with massive frescoes.

Mycenaean pottery shows Minoan plant and animal life and the Mycenaean fascination with warrior scenes and warfare. Over time, they added more patterns and designs and left open spaces on their jars. While plain clay vessels were affordable to everyone, decorated jars catered to an elite clientele.

The Mycenaean warrior elites were buried with death masks—a funerary representation of the deceased. The ***Death Mask of Agamemnon***, a 16th-century BCE gold funerary mask named after the **legendary king of Mycenae** from Homer's *The **Iliad*, is the most famous death mask.

- Mycenaean art is characterized by its stylized and abstract forms, in contrast to the more naturalistic style of Minoan art.

- Mycenaean metalwork was highly developed, with examples such as intricate jewelry, armor, and sculptures.

### Mycenaean Fortifications

Mycenaean fortifications were architectural structures built with techniques such as **Cyclopean masonry to protect palaces and cities from invaders**. The most notable example is the ***Lions Gate *****in Mycenae**, and other examples include **the** **Walls of Tiryns** and **the Citadel of Mycenae**.

**The Treasury of Atreus,** located in Mycenae, Greece and dating back to circa 1300-1250 BCE, showcases impressive Mycenaean fortifications. One notable feature is the use of corbelled vaulting, a technique where stones are stacked and gradually projected inward to create a domed roof, covering a large open area. This architectural innovation allowed for the construction of expansive and impressive tombs, such as the Treasury of Atreus, highlighting the advanced engineering skills and architectural achievements of the Mycenaean civilization.

In keeping with their warrior culture, the Mycenaeans built walls of massive rough-cut stones stacked tightly together with no binding agent like cement. The fortifications of Mycenae were known as ***Cyclopean walls,**** *and they measured about 45 feet tall and at least 20 feet thick.

The Mycenaeans also excelled at the corbelling technique to create the **corbel arch **wherein rows of stones extend slightly past and under one another, forming a relieving triangle, an open space that keeps weight off the lintel. The **corbel vault**, in comparison, is a series of corbel arches placed together to make an open space or walkway.

### The Decline of Mycenaean Civilization

With the Bronze Age Collapse of the 12th century BCE began the decline of Mycenaean Greece, but the vibrant material culture, art, and architecture of the Mycenaeans would lay the foundation for the rise of Western Civilization through their influence on the Ancient Greeks.

## F. Classical Greece

Subsequently, after the end of the Mycenaean civilization around the 12th century BCE, the people and territories of ancient Greece slowly emerged anew. ### Classical Greek Sculptures 

#### What defines classical Greek sculpture?

Classical Greek sculpture refers to the sculptural works created during the Classical period of ancient Greece, which spanned from the 5th to the 4th century BCE.

Classical Greek sculpture is characterized by idealized forms, naturalistic portrayal of the human body, balance and contrapposto, narrative and mythological themes, the use of marble as the preferred medium, and integration into architecture. It emphasizes beauty, proportion, and harmony while depicting gods, heroes, and mythological scenes. These sculptures have had a lasting influence on Western art and are celebrated for their artistic achievements and aesthetic ideals.

### Kritios Boy (c. 480 BCE)

The *Kritios Boy*, created by the sculptor Kritios, marks a significant shift in Greek statuary and is regarded as one of the earliest examples of Classical Greek sculpture. This marble statue is known for introducing the** concept of contrapposto**; a pose that creates a sense of naturalistic movement and balance.

In contrast to the rigid stance of earlier Egyptian and Greek statues, the *Kritios Boy* displays a harmonious and fluid posture. The figure's right hip dips, shifting the weight to the left leg and creating a lifelike sense of motion. The head is turned and tilted, adding a subtle touch of naturalism to the sculpture, capturing the human body in a more dynamic and realistic manner. Additionally, the statue’s face imparts an emotionally restrained mannerism, reflecting the** idealized aesthetic of Classical Greek art**.

The revolutionary contrapposto stance depicted in the *Kritios Boy *would reemerge in art during the later periods, such as the Middle Ages and Renaissance, as there was a renewed appreciation for the classical artistic tradition. 

### Discobolus (460–450 BCE)

***Discobolus**** *by Myron of Eleutherae introduced greater boldness of pose and a perfect rhythm, subordinating the parts to the whole. The sculptor was an Athenian from the mid-5th century BCE. He worked almost exclusively in bronze and was popular for his work on representations of athletes.

The sculpture **depicts an athlete**, caught in a moment of intense focus, preparing to throw a discus. The *Discobolus *represents the **idealized human form of a Greek athlete**, with exaggerated musculature and an athletic build and was made using the **lost-wax casting method**.

| **Study Note: **Discobolus Myron's *Discobolus*, or "discus thrower," was the first known piece to successfully portray a moment of physical balance and harmony. The original *Discobolus*, crafted in bronze, has been lost to history and is known only through its Roman marble copy. |

### The Doryphoros  (440 BCE)

***The Doryphoros***, also known as the “Spear-Bearer” statue, is a highly influential ancient Greek sculpture created by famous Greek sculptor **Polykleitos**.

### What does the statue depict, and how does it reflect Greek art ideals?

The statue depicts a **young man in mid-stride carrying a spear** over his left shoulder. The statue reflects the **importance of balance and realism** in Greek art, as Polykleitos depicts the young man with the dimensions expected for the** ideal male** form, as determined by the mathematical and scientific philosophies of the ancient Greeks.

**Polykleitos was an influential Greek sculptor** born in Argos on the Greek peninsula of Peloponnesus in the 5th century BCE. He exemplified the ancient Greek ideals concerning the human body and a desire to create symmetry through bodily proportions and the balance of physical features. Some of Polykleitos' other important sculptures include the *Diadoumenos *(“Youth Tying a Headband”) and the *Mantua Apollo*.

### What is the Canon of Polykleitos, and how is it incorporated in the Doryphoros?

The Canon of Polykleitos was a **mathematical and scientific model for depicting the ideal human form**. The Canon incorporated a combination of both symmetry and proportion. *The Doryphoros* by Polykleitos represented a physical example of his Canon, providing guidelines for the ideal proportions of the human body.

### Classical Greek Architecture: Elements of Design

Greek architecture is known for its precise mathematical and scientific approach, which resulted in consistent styles over long periods. Three main elements make up the design of Greek architecture, including the entablature, capital, and pediment. 

#### The three main elements of architectural relief are entablature, capital, and pediment. 

First, an **entablature** is a **horizontal element** that is on top of the columns of Greco-Roman Classical style buildings or similar structural supports in non-Classical buildings. The entablature is divided into three sections:

- **Architrave: **The bottom horizontal base

- **Frieze: **The decorative element that may include relief sculptures

- **Cornice: **The decorative horizontal element below the roofline

Second is the **capital, **the structural columns (the upper base of the column is called the capital), which supports the entablature.

Lastly, **the pediment **is a triangular gable — a wall that extends to fill the space underneath the two slopes of a pitched roof — which is an element of Classical and Neoclassical architecture.

Moreover, the Greeks developed three orders: the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. It became a fundamental part of Rome’s architecture and, subsequently, much of Europe and the United States. These orders were developed in different parts of Greece and at different times. The difference between the columns, their capitals, and the entablature above them define the distinction between the orders.

| **The Doric Order:** The simplest of the orders which features smooth or fluted columns with circular capitals. Above the simple columns, the **entablature **elements add a more intricate decorative accent. |  |

| **The Ionic Order:** The Ionic column has *volutes *(Latin for scroll) as a decorative element at the top of the capital. A **narrative frieze** is intended to run the length of the structure as part of the entablature's design. |  |
| **The Corinthian Order:** This is the most decorative form and is named for the Greek city of Corinth. It has elaborately carved capitals with an **acanthus leaf motif**. |  |

Strength and beauty through logic and symmetry were primary themes in the architectural designs of the Greeks.  **Hippodamus of Miletus** (c. 498–408 BCE), who is credited with establishing a formal method of city planning based on these vaunted Greek themes, designed the town of Piraeus, which served as a commercial port for Athens, Olynthus, Priene, and Miletus, and which was renowned for being the “ideal city.”

### The Parthenon (447-438 BCE)

Parthenon was the first temple to be built entirely of marble and is located in the Acropolis of Athens. It was a temple that was dedicated to the goddess Athena. The name Parthenon comes from “*Parthemos*” in Greek meaning “virgin”, or “innocent maiden”, a reference to the chaste goddess.  

The Parthenon was built between 447-438 BCE during the Athenian Empire in the High Classical period of ancient Greece. It is a **Doric** building with some **Ionic** architectural features. The Doric temple consists of a rectangular floor plan with a series of low steps on every side and a **colonnade **of Doric columns extending around the periphery of the entire structure. The roof has Doric triangular **gables **called **pediments**, decorated with sculptures, and an Ionic frieze, or band of relief sculptures, that reaches the whole way around the roof. Four Ionic columns support the roof of the smallest room, the *opisthodomos*, or “inner shrine”.

It uses a 9:4 ratio in many of its components and is 101 feet wide by 228 feet long. The whole building is based on a **harmonious numerical ratio of golden rectangles**; however, the construction is quite irregular. Due to an optical illusion that comes from all the columns being behind one another, the corner columns would have looked thinner if they were made the same thickness as the other columns. To counteract this they were made thicker, providing an intentional optical illusion that, as a result, makes them look the same thickness as the other columns.

It has the remnants of numerous historic and architecturally significant ancient structures, the most well-known of which is the Parthenon.

*The Acropolis of Athens was an ancient citadel located on an extremely rocky outcrop above the city of Athens.*

## G. Hellenistic Greece

### What was the Hellenistic Period?

The Hellenistic period of ancient Greece (323–31 BCE) marked a **significant shift in the artistic and cultural landscape of the region**. During the reign of Alexander the Great, Greek art and culture spread throughout his vast empire, resulting in a **blending of Greek styles with those of other cultures, **developing into what would become the Hellenistic period after his death in 323 BCE. This period saw the **emergence of new artistic forms and techniques**, including realistic portraiture, complex sculptures, and intricate mosaics. Hellenistic Greece also witnessed the **construction of impressive architectural marvels**, such as the Library of Alexandria and the Colossus of Rhodes. The legacy of Hellenistic art and architecture can still be seen today, influencing and inspiring artists and designers around the world.

**During the Hellenistic period**, the Greeks referred to themselves as Hellenes and were composed of independent city-states. Athens established a democracy, and the Greeks placed a great emphasis on the human form, even portraying their gods and goddesses as human-like. They aimed to create the perfect individual by achieving a balance between intellectual and physical discipline. **They regarded the human body as beautiful, perfectly balanced, and harmonious, and this belief was evident in their paintings and sculptures.** This emphasis on balance, harmony, and symmetry extended into their other achievements as well, such as in architecture, mathematics, science, philosophy, and poetry.

### How did Hellenistic sculptors make their pieces look as human as possible?

Hellenistic period artists used **dynamic silhouettes and sinuous forms** to suggest movement, resulting in sculptures that were more expressive and exaggerated than those of previous eras. 

One of the most famous examples of this style is ***Laocoön and His Sons***** (27 BCE–68 CE),** which depicts three figures in a dramatic, action-packed scene. This **focus on movement** also influenced the period's emphasis on **realistic anatomy**, with artists breaking away from the rigid poses of earlier eras and instead creating sculptures inspired by real human postures. Known as **contrapposto**, this pose was **asymmetrical** and conveyed a **sense of movement** through realistic weight distribution and an S-shaped body.

Hellenistic sculpture also features **ornate details**, particularly in the area of drapery. Sculptors adorned their figures with "fabric" to accentuate movement, emphasize lifelike anatomy, and showcase their sculpting skills. This "wet drapery" technique, which first appeared during the Classical period, was adapted and refined by Hellenistic artists.

### The Parthenon Frieze (443-438 BCE)

The *Parthenon Frieze* is **a sculptural work** that adorned the upper part of the outer walls of the Parthenon, a temple dedicated to the goddess Athena on the Acropolis of Athens. It was** **created between 443-438 BCE by the sculptor Phidias and his assistants.

The frieze depicts a **procession of people, animals, and gods**, all dressed in traditional Greek clothing and engaged in various activities, such as carrying offerings, leading horses, playing music, and conversing with each other. The procession is believed to represent the **Great Panathenaic Festival**, a major Athenian festival that honored Athena, which took place every four years.

*The Parthenon Frieze* is widely regarded as one of the greatest achievements of ancient Greek art. It is notable for its high level of artistic and technical skill, as well as its innovative use of **perspective and dramatic composition**. The figures in the frieze are depicted in a **continuous narrative** that unfolds across the entire length of the temple, creating a dynamic and immersive experience for viewers.

### Aphrodite of Knidos (4th century BCE)

***The Aphrodite of Knidos***** by Praxiteles**, is a renowned Greek sculpture and a significant masterpiece of ancient art. It gained fame as the first nude representation of a female goddess in a devotional context and was crafted from exquisite marble. The sculpture caused a sensation when installed in a sacred area on the island of Knidos, captivating viewers with its beauty and revolutionary depiction. 

The statue, also known as the *Venus Pudica* or **"****modest Venus,****"** features the goddess Aphrodite covering her pubic area with her right hand, adding a touch of modesty to the otherwise exposed body. While the original Greek sculpture is no longer extant, Roman artists recreated the image based on descriptions and Greek influences, providing insights into its likely appearance. 

The sculpture's representation of the female form challenged traditional norms and marked a pivotal moment in artistic conventions. Commissioned as a cult statue for a temple, it depicted Aphrodite preparing for a ritual bath, symbolizing her **purification and renewal** of purity. The positioning of the hands serves a dual purpose, both shielding her modesty and drawing attention to her exposed nudity. *The Aphrodite of Knidos* represents a significant milestone in the depiction of the female body and continues to inspire awe and admiration as a symbol of beauty and artistic evolution in ancient Greece.

### Venus de Milo (130-100 BCE)

The *Aphrodite of Milos*, also known as the* Venus de Milo*, was sculpted by Alexandros of Antioch during the Hellenistic period. **Aphrodite, the goddess of Love**, served as the inspiration for this iconic statue. In contrast to earlier depictions of Aphrodite, which emphasized modesty, Hellenistic sculptors like Alexandros explored the eroticism and sensuality of the female form.

The *Venus de Milo* is a provocative sculpture that openly embraces the sexuality of the **nude female figure**. It was designed to entice and tease the viewer, with its idealized beauty and alluring pose. The statue holds an apple in its left hand, symbolizing the prize awarded to Aphrodite by the mythological Greek hero Paris when he declared her the most beautiful goddess.

The statue derives its name from the Greek island of Melos (Milos), where it was discovered in 1820 and later acquired by the Louvre Museum in Paris, France. Its missing arms have long been a subject of intrigue and debate. While the original purpose and identity of the statue remain uncertain, the sensual and half-naked body, as well as the jewelry found near the sculpture, led to the conclusion that it represents Aphrodite, or Venus in Roman mythology.

### Seated Boxer (330-50 BCE)

*The Seated Boxer*, also known as the *Boxer at Rest*, is a notable **ancient bronze sculpture** depicting a seated and naked boxer. The statue **captures a moment just after a boxing match**, showcasing the physical toll and injuries endured by the athlete. With his head turned to the right, the boxer's face exhibits bruises, cuts, and a broken nose. His “cauliflower-ears”, a common boxing injury, bear the marks of previous fights, while fresh bloody cuts adorn his face and ears from his most recent bout.

The boxer's muscular physique, full beard, and mature appearance reflect his experience as an athlete. Despite his exhaustion, the tension in his arm and leg muscles suggests readiness for another confrontation. The sculpture portrays the boxer in a seated position, with his arms resting on his knees, wearing ancient Greek-style boxing gloves, consisting of leather strips attached to a ring around the knuckles and padded with wool. 

*The Seated Boxer* is a testament to the artist's skill in capturing the physical and emotional realities of a boxer's life. It highlights the physical toll, injuries, and determination of the athlete, providing a glimpse into the world of ancient Greek sports and the rigorous nature of boxing. Today, this remarkable sculpture is admired for its lifelike representation and the insight it offers into the ancient sporting culture.

### Laocoön and His Sons (27 BCE–68 CE)

The statue of *Laocoön and His Sons *by  Agesander, Athenodorus, and Polydorus has been one of the most famous ancient sculptures since it was excavated in 1506 with Michelangelo himself present, and was then placed on public display in the Vatican Museums, where it remains. This piece is a prime example of a “sculpture in the round” which means it is meant to be viewed from all angles and not just from the front. 

The figures are nearly life-size and the group is around 6 feet, 7 inches in height, showing the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons **Antiphantes and Thymbraeus** being attacked by serpents sent by the gods to punish them.

### How has Hellenistic sculpture influenced art movements throughout history?

The lasting influence of Hellenistic sculpture can be seen in **its impact on later movements and genres**. Italian artists like Michelangelo were inspired by its **emphasis on anatomy** during the Renaissance, while Bernini found **inspiration in its dynamic movement** during the Baroque era. In the 19th century, sculptor Giovanni Strazza employed the "wet drapery" technique to create the *Veiled Virgin*. These examples, along with many others, illustrate the enduring legacy of Hellenistic sculpture.

## H. Ancient Rome: Kingdom, Republic, and Empire (753 BCE–476 CE)

Rome, founded in **753 BCE** by brothers Romulus and Remus (so legend has it), has been the site of some of the most significant events in human history. It was a center of power and influence for centuries and the world's largest city during the Roman Empire at its height that included the entire Italian peninsula, much of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Historically, the Roman Empire is divided into **Republican Rome** (509–27 BCE), when Rome was governed by the aristocracy, and** Imperial Rome** (27 BCE–476 CE), when Rome was ruled by emperors.

During the** Republican Rome**, archaic culture continued, and the conquest of Greece, becoming a part of the Roman province, led to the blend of Greek and Roman art and culture. During this period, Roman artworks began to appear in higher numbers, ultimately leading to an identifiable Roman artistic culture. 

Meanwhile, during the era of **Imperial Rome**, each leader’s reign emphasized different art forms. For instance, under Augustan (27 BCE–14 CE), the fusion of the Greek styles and Italian naturalism prevailed. The Julio-Claudian dynasty (14–68 CE), by contrast, is characterized by extravagance, and imperial portraiture which was used for propagandistic purposes. Lastly, during the period of Flavian (69–98 CE), Rome underwent major rebuilding, including the construction of new aqueducts and canals.

The Romans produced different art forms, including painting, mosaic, sculpture, and architecture, and were probably best known for their sculptures, created to commemorate Rome's conquests through narrative reliefs and to glorify its leaders, and their incredible feets of engineering.  Some of the common characteristics of their works can still be seen today, like the Doric columns used in public buildings, lifelike statues, murals, and mosaic floors in homes. The influence of Roman art was highly prevalent in the Italian Renaissance and even in contemporary art forms and architecture.
